warmup.q: You time 100 million calls of Math.sqrt(x) in a loop with System.nanoTime() and throw each result away. After a few rounds the loop reports 0.0000 ns per call. What is the best explanation?
options: Your CPU computes square roots in well under a nanosecond
The JIT saw that the results were never used and removed the work from the loop
System.nanoTime() is too coarse to measure such short calls
The JVM cached the result of the first call
warmup.why: No CPU does a square root in 0.0000 ns. Once C2 compiled the loop, it proved that nothing used the result of Math.sqrt(x) and deleted the call: that's dead-code elimination, the first section's topic. nanoTime() is precise enough for a 100-million-lap loop, and the JVM keeps no cache of Math.sqrt results.

opening:
Picture a restaurant that wants to know which of two cooks makes the house soup faster. The manager hands each cook an order, starts a stopwatch, and stops it when the bowl lands on the counter. Simple enough. But one cook has noticed that nobody ever eats the test bowls, so they stop making them. The stopwatch reads zero.

A loop timed with System.nanoTime() gives the JIT, the JVM's compiler for busy code, the same chance. In this lesson's first demo, a loop of 100 million square roots reported 0.0000 ns per call. The work wasn't fast; it was missing, because nothing used the result.

The trap is easy to fall into, because those numbers look so precise. Lesson 2 asked you to trust a JMH benchmark that counted types at a call site; now JMH has to earn that trust. In this lesson, we'll watch a hand-made timing loop lie, let JMH build the loop instead, learn the two rules that fix most broken benchmarks, and find a number steady enough to check on a busy machine. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a cook who stops making the test bowls nobody eats, and a stopwatch that reads zero. A nanoTime loop invites the JIT to do the same. JMH runs the fair taste test instead: a warmed-up kitchen, a fresh one for each fork, unpredictable ingredients in @State fields, and a judge who eats every result.

Now search your own tests for System.nanoTime() next to an assert. Each one is a timing check that will fail at random on a busy build machine, or a benchmark that measured less than it claims.

Next, we'll leave the single thread behind: why can two threads that never touch the same field still slow each other down?

sections.h: A nanoTime loop measures the optimizer, not your code
sections.html:
Here's the benchmark almost everyone writes first. A benchmark is a small program that measures how long some code takes. This one is as simple as it gets: read the clock, call the code many times, read the clock again.

Java
long t0 = System.nanoTime();
for (int i = 0; i < 100_000_000; i++) {
    Math.sqrt(x);                      // result discarded
}
long t1 = System.nanoTime();
System.out.printf("%.4f ns/op%n", (t1 - t0) / 1e8);
Kotlin
val t0 = System.nanoTime()
for (i in 0 until 100_000_000) {
    sqrt(x)                            // result discarded
}
val t1 = System.nanoTime()
println("%.4f ns/op".format((t1 - t0) / 1e8))

NanoLoop, in the Try it, runs that loop five times, next to a second loop that adds every result to a sum and prints the sum. On JDK 25 it printed (with the sum trimmed off):

round 1: discarded 0.0678 ns/op, used 3.3919 ns/op
round 2: discarded 0.2053 ns/op, used 3.0171 ns/op
round 3: discarded 0.0000 ns/op, used 3.3148 ns/op
round 4: discarded 0.0000 ns/op, used 3.2549 ns/op
round 5: discarded 0.0000 ns/op, used 3.5381 ns/op

Zero nanoseconds per square root. That's faster than light, and a little suspicious. The second loop settled at about 3 ns per call, which is believable for a square root and an addition on a busy machine.

The first loop measured nothing because, once C2 (the JIT's optimizing compiler) had compiled it, there was nothing left to measure. C2 proved that nobody used the result of Math.sqrt(x), so it deleted the call, and then the empty loop. That's dead-code elimination: work whose result nobody uses can go. It's the cook skipping the bowl nobody eats.

Here the picture breaks, and in a useful way. A cook who skips a bowl knows they're cutting a corner. The JIT isn't cheating at all. Removing unused work is exactly its job, and our benchmark gave it permission.

Dead code is one of several ways a hand-made loop lies:

  • If the input is a constant, C2 can compute the answer at compile time, and you end up timing the load of one number. That's constant folding: the cook who gets the same order every time makes it before the doors open.
  • The first rounds run in the interpreter, which reads bytecode one instruction at a time, and in OSR code, a loop compiled while it runs, as lesson 1 showed. A benchmark written as one long loop in main keeps measuring OSR code.
  • The JIT unrolls loops and moves work out of them. JMH's own sample on loops reports the measured cost of an addition falling "up to the point we do each addition with 1/20 ns, well beyond what hardware can actually do".

A broken benchmark can also print a believable number, which is worse. Change the discarded call to Math.log(x). On JDK 21, that loop was never removed: it reported 10 to 13 ns per call, round after round. On JDK 25, it dropped to 0.0000 by round 3, like the square root. Same source, two JDKs, two stories. Whether the JIT can remove a call depends on what it can prove, and you can't see that from the outside.

A timing loop you wrote by hand measures whatever the JIT left behind. Don't trust its number.

So we need a loop the JIT can't hollow out, warmed up, in a fresh JVM, timed with care. Writing that by hand is a project of its own. Fortunately, the OpenJDK team already wrote it.

try.title: Watch the work disappear
steps: Read NanoLoop. Predict both columns for round 1 and round 5.
Run it. Then run the Kotlin twin.
Change the discarded loop to Math.log(x) in either version and run it again. If you have two JDKs installed, try both.

code.title: NanoLoop.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l03; /** * The benchmark everyone writes first: a loop timed with System.nanoTime(). * Round by round it measures the same thing, twice: once with the result thrown away, * once with the result added to a sum that gets printed. */ public class NanoLoop { public static void main(String[] args) { double x = 2.0; for (int round = 1; round <= 5; round++) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 100_000_000; i++) { Math.sqrt(x); // result discarded } long t1 = System.nanoTime(); double sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 100_000_000; i++) { sum += Math.sqrt(x + i); // result used } long t2 = System.nanoTime(); System.out.printf("round %d: discarded %.4f ns/op, used %.4f ns/op (sum %.1f)%n", round, (t1 - t0) / 1e8, (t2 - t1) / 1e8, sum); } } }

alt.title: NanoLoop.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l03 import kotlin.math.sqrt // Kotlin twin of NanoLoop.java: the same naive nanoTime benchmark, with the result // thrown away and with the result used. fun main() { val x = 2.0 for (round in 1..5) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() for (i in 0 until 100_000_000) { sqrt(x) // result discarded } val t1 = System.nanoTime() var sum = 0.0 for (i in 0 until 100_000_000) { sum += sqrt(x + i) // result used } val t2 = System.nanoTime() println("round %d: discarded %.4f ns/op, used %.4f ns/op (sum %.1f)" .format(round, (t1 - t0) / 1e8, (t2 - t1) / 1e8, sum)) } }

try.expect: The discarded column starts below 1 ns and reads 0.0000 by round 3; the used column stays near 3 ns. Kotlin does the same. With Math.log, the result depends on the JDK: on JDK 21 the discarded loop reported 10 to 13 ns per call and never reached zero, while on JDK 25 it reached 0.0000 by round 3. Neither loop tells you the real cost of the method.

video.title: A nanoTime loop measures the optimizer: dead code, constant folding, and the loop JMH builds instead

sections.h: JMH builds the measuring loop for you
sections.html:
That tool is JMH, the Java Microbenchmark Harness: the OpenJDK project's code for running microbenchmarks, benchmarks of small pieces of code. It calls your method, times it and reports the result. Version 1.37, from August 2023, is still the latest release, and it's the version in this course's Gradle build.

You write a method and mark it @Benchmark. JMH's annotation processor, a plug-in that runs while javac compiles, generates the measuring loop around it, written to defeat the tricks from the last section. A runner then executes it in fresh JVMs.

Think of it as the taste test done fairly. A fair test warms the kitchen up first and throws away the practice dishes. It uses ingredients the cook can't predict, so nothing can be made in advance. A judge eats every dish, so none can be skipped. And it runs in a fresh kitchen each day, so yesterday's habits don't leak into today. JMH gives you each of those. Here's a complete benchmark for the report service's reading time:

Java
@State(Scope.Thread)
@BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime)
@OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)
@Warmup(iterations = 5, time = 1)          // 5 x 1 s, results thrown away
@Measurement(iterations = 5, time = 1)     // 5 x 1 s, results kept
@Fork(2)                                   // two fresh JVMs
public class ReadingBench {
    long words = 1_234;                    // input: a non-final field of the state object

    @Benchmark
    public long seconds() {
        return ReadingMath.readingSeconds(words);   // returned: JMH consumes it
    }
}
Kotlin
@State(Scope.Thread)
@BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime)
@OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)
@Warmup(iterations = 5, time = 1)
@Measurement(iterations = 5, time = 1)
@Fork(2)
open class ReadingBench {                  // JMH's generated code extends it, so it can't be final
    var words = 1_234L                     // var: an input nobody can predict

    @Benchmark
    fun seconds(): Long = ReadingMath.readingSeconds(words)
}

What each piece does:

  • @State(Scope.Thread): one instance of the class per benchmark thread (a thread is one line of work inside a program, and JMH can run several at once). Its fields are your inputs, the ingredients the cook can't predict.
  • @Setup: a method that prepares the state outside the measured time. Level.Trial, the default, runs it once per fork.
  • @Warmup and @Measurement: how many iterations, and how long each lasts. Warm-up results, the practice dishes, are thrown away.
  • @Fork: how many fresh JVMs to run in, the fresh kitchens. A new JVM starts with a clean profile, the JIT's notes on what the code did, so one benchmark can't skew the next. @Fork(0) runs inside the JVM that launched it, which brings back every problem of the hand-made loop.
  • @BenchmarkMode: Throughput (operations per unit of time, the default), AverageTime, SampleTime or SingleShotTime.
  • @Param: runs the benchmark once per value, as lesson 2's MegamorphicBench did with its number of types.

The return value is the judge who eats the dish: JMH consumes it, so the JIT has to compute it.

The Kotlin class has to be open, because JMH's generated classes extend it. A Kotlin build also needs a plugin, such as kotlinx-benchmark, to generate the JMH code for Kotlin classes. So this course keeps its benchmarks in Java, and drives them from Kotlin where that helps.

The JMH 1.37 defaults are 5 forks, each with 5 warm-up and 5 measurement iterations of 10 seconds: more than eight minutes per benchmark method. JMH is in no hurry, on purpose. The demos in this track use iterations of 100 to 300 ms so they finish quickly. That's fine for seeing a trap, and too short for deciding anything.

You can run benchmarks from a main method with JMH's Runner and OptionsBuilder, as the demos do, or from a JMH jar with command-line flags such as -f 2 -wi 5 -i 5 -prof gc. Since JDK 24, JMH 1.37 makes the JVM print a few WARNING lines about sun.misc.Unsafe, an internal JDK class it uses. They don't affect the results.

The harness is honest. Our benchmarks still have to give it honest inputs, and that's where most broken benchmarks go wrong.

try.title: Five ways to measure one square root
steps: Read TrapsBench. Predict which of the five benchmarks will score about the same as baseline.
Run it (under 10 seconds). Then run the Kotlin twin, which runs two of the five with JMH's full output, so you can watch the warm-up and measurement iterations go by.
Change double x = 2.0; to final double x = 2.0; and run the Java version again. Which benchmarks change?

code.title: TrapsBench.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l03; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Benchmark; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.BenchmarkMode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Fork; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Measurement; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Mode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.OutputTimeUnit; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Scope; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.State; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Warmup; import org.openjdk.jmh.infra.Blackhole; import org.openjdk.jmh.results.RunResult; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.Runner; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.OptionsBuilder; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.VerboseMode; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** The same Math.sqrt measured five ways. The iterations are far shorter than JMH's defaults, so treat the numbers as rough. */ @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 2, time = 100, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Measurement(iterations = 3, time = 100, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Fork(1) public class TrapsBench { double x = 2.0; // input from a non-final @State field static final double CONSTANT = 2.0; // input the JIT knows at compile time @Benchmark public void baseline() { } // the harness on its own @Benchmark public void sqrtDiscarded() { Math.sqrt(x); } // result thrown away @Benchmark public double sqrtReturned() { return Math.sqrt(x); } // JMH consumes the return value @Benchmark public void sqrtBlackhole(Blackhole bh) { bh.consume(Math.sqrt(x)); } @Benchmark public double sqrtOfConstant() { return Math.sqrt(CONSTANT); } // folded before it runs public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { var options = new OptionsBuilder() .include(TrapsBench.class.getName()) .verbosity(VerboseMode.SILENT) .build(); System.out.printf("%-16s %10s %10s%n", "Benchmark", "ns/op", "error"); for (RunResult r : new Runner(options).run()) { var s = r.getPrimaryResult(); System.out.printf("%-16s %10.3f %10.3f%n", r.getParams().getBenchmark().replaceAll(".*\\.", ""), s.getScore(), s.getScoreError()); } } }

alt.title: TrapsBench.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l03 // JMH benchmarks must be Java classes in this lab (the annotation processor runs on Java only). // This Kotlin twin runs the same Java benchmark through JMH's Runner API, but with JMH's // normal output, so you can see every warm-up and measurement iteration as it happens. import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.Runner import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.OptionsBuilder import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.VerboseMode fun main() { val options = OptionsBuilder() .include(TrapsBench::class.java.name + ".sqrt(Discarded|Returned)") // a regex: two of the five .verbosity(VerboseMode.NORMAL) .build() Runner(options).run() }

try.expect: sqrtDiscarded and sqrtOfConstant usually land on top of baseline: 0.4 to 0.9 ns on the busy course machine, with error bars bigger than the scores. sqrtReturned and sqrtBlackhole take about 2 to 5 ns. With final double x = 2.0, javac copies 2.0 into every method, so every benchmark drops to the baseline, sqrtReturned and sqrtBlackhole included: 0.44 and 0.47 ns in the run here. The Kotlin twin's log shows # Blackhole mode: compiler (auto-detected ...) and ends with JMH's "REMEMBER: The numbers below are just data" warning.

sections.h: Two rules: consume every result, read inputs from non-final fields
sections.html:
Two rules fix most broken benchmarks, and the three broken benchmarks in the lab each break one of them.

First, every result must reach JMH. The simplest way is to return it, because JMH consumes return values. When there are two results, combine them, or pass each one to a Blackhole, a JMH object whose consume method takes a value and makes sure the JIT has to compute it:

Java
@Benchmark
public void readingAndSpeaking(Blackhole bh) {
    bh.consume(ReadingMath.readingSeconds(words));
    bh.consume(ReadingMath.speakingSeconds(words));
}
Kotlin
@Benchmark
fun readingAndSpeaking(bh: Blackhole) {
    bh.consume(ReadingMath.readingSeconds(words))
    bh.consume(ReadingMath.speakingSeconds(words))
}

JMH's sample on Blackholes adds that if you have one result, you should return it: "Do not make your benchmark code less readable with explicit Blackholes!" On JDK 17 and later, JMH uses compiler blackholes, where the JIT itself treats consume as "this value is used, and nothing else". The log header says so, as # Blackhole mode: compiler, and JMH warns that results from different Blackhole modes can't be compared.

Second, inputs must come from non-final instance fields of the @State object. A final field with a constant initializer is a compile-time constant in Java, so javac copies the value into your method. javap on the lab's broken ConstantInputBench shows it:

public long seconds();
   0: ldc2_w  #7      // long 1234l   <- the field is gone; the number is baked in
   3: invokestatic    ReadingMath.readingSeconds:(J)J
   6: lreturn

From there C2 can fold the whole calculation into one number. JMH's constant-folding sample puts it bluntly: "IDEs will say 'Look, this field could be final'. Don't. Trust. Them." A static final input has the same problem, which is what sqrtOfConstant shows in the Try it above. Even the judge can't help then. With final double x, sqrtBlackhole dropped to the baseline too, because a Blackhole can't stop the cook from making the dish in advance.

You can check both rules against a baseline: an empty @Benchmark method that measures the harness alone, 0.6 to 0.9 ns in the busy runs here. A benchmark that scores like the baseline is measuring nothing, whatever its name says. In those runs, the discarded and the constant square roots sat right on it, and the returned and consumed ones took two to seven times as long. The absolute numbers change from run to run on a busy machine. Which benchmarks sit on the baseline doesn't.

Check yourself: a benchmark returns ReadingMath.readingSeconds(words * PAGES), where PAGES is a static final long and words is a non-final @State field. Can C2 fold the whole result into a constant? (No. PAGES is known, but words can change between calls, so the calculation has to run.)

A benchmark that scores like an empty method is measuring nothing. Put a baseline next to it.

Even an honest benchmark has one weak spot, though: look at the error column on any of these runs. There's a steadier number to watch.

sections.h: Count bytes with -prof gc, because they don't wobble
sections.html:
Time is the noisiest thing you can measure. On a shared machine, the error bar of a short JMH run is often bigger than the score itself. Allocation is different. Allocation is the memory a method asks for when it creates objects. For the same code and the same input, a method allocates the same number of bytes every time. JMH's GC profiler reports it as gc.alloc.rate.norm, in bytes per operation (B/op). GC stands for the garbage collector, the part of the JVM that frees memory nobody uses. You turn the profiler on with -prof gc on the command line, or addProfiler(GCProfiler.class) in code.

The report service counts words all day, so WordCountBench counts the words in 100 lines of text, two ways. One splits each line with String.split(" ") and counts the pieces. The other walks the characters and counts where words start:

Java
@Benchmark
public long wordsBySplit() {                // short and clear, and every word becomes a new String
    long total = 0;
    for (String line : lines) total += line.split(" ").length;
    return total;
}

@Benchmark
public long wordsByScan() {                 // walks the characters and counts where words start
    long total = 0;
    for (String line : lines) {
        boolean inWord = false;
        for (int i = 0; i < line.length(); i++) {
            boolean letter = line.charAt(i) != ' ';
            if (letter && !inWord) total++;
            inWord = letter;
        }
    }
    return total;
}
Kotlin
fun wordsBySplit(): Long {
    var total = 0L
    for (line in lines) total += line.split(' ').size   // Kotlin's split returns a List of new Strings
    return total
}

fun wordsByScan(): Long {
    var total = 0L
    for (line in lines) {
        var inWord = false
        for (c in line) {
            val letter = c != ' '
            if (letter && !inWord) total++
            inWord = letter
        }
    }
    return total
}

Two runs on the busy course machine, JDK 25:

Benchmark             ns/op      error           B/op    error
wordsByScan          6906.4    16886.8          0.158    0.387
wordsBySplit        41270.4   301449.2      54400.943    7.286

wordsByScan          7485.8    11955.5          0.173    0.297
wordsBySplit        32185.0    70883.8      54425.122  769.564

Look at the error columns. Every time error is bigger than its score, from one and a half to seven times bigger, so the times say almost nothing. The bytes barely moved: about 54,400 bytes per call, 544 per line, and the same on JDK 21. split builds a new String for each of a line's nine words, plus an array to hand them back in. The scan allocates nothing at all. (The second run's ±770 is the profiler's own sampling showing through, and it's still under 2% of the score.)

split is the clear choice for most code. In the report service's busiest loop, though, 54 KB for every 100 lines adds up, and lesson 7 follows an allocation problem like it from start to finish.

That steadiness makes B/op the number to check automatically, in CI (continuous integration, the build server that runs your tests on every change). A test can't assert "under 30 µs" without failing at random on a busy build machine. It can assert "under 300 bytes per call", and lesson 7's lab does exactly that. Keep time measurements for quiet, dedicated machines, with several forks.

Time wobbles on a busy machine; bytes per operation don't. Put the bytes in your checks.

JMH has more profilers. -lprof lists the ones your machine supports. -prof stack samples thread stacks, the chains of method calls each thread is in. The perf family (perfnorm, perfasm) needs the Linux perf tool and shows hardware counters and the generated machine code. Every JMH run ends with a reminder worth reading once: "The numbers below are just data. To gain reusable insights, you need to follow up on why the numbers are the way they are."

Everything in this lesson ran on one thread. Programs have many, and two threads can slow each other down even when they never touch the same field.

try.title: Count the bytes
steps: Predict the B/op of each benchmark in WordCountBench, roughly.
Run it (about 7 seconds). Compare the error columns for time and for bytes.
Run the Kotlin twin. It writes the same two counts in Kotlin and counts bytes with the JVM's per-thread allocation counter instead of JMH. Why might its split number differ from Java's?

code.title: WordCountBench.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l03; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Benchmark; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.BenchmarkMode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Fork; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Measurement; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Mode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.OutputTimeUnit; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Scope; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Setup; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.State; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Warmup; import org.openjdk.jmh.profile.GCProfiler; import org.openjdk.jmh.results.RunResult; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.Runner; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.OptionsBuilder; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.VerboseMode; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** Counts the words in 100 lines of text two ways, String.split and a character scan, with JMH's GC profiler on. */ @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 2, time = 300, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Measurement(iterations = 3, time = 300, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Fork(1) public class WordCountBench { String[] lines; @Setup public void setup() { // built once per fork, outside the measurement lines = new String[100]; for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) lines[i] = "the report counts every word on line number " + i; } @Benchmark public long wordsBySplit() { // short and clear, and every word becomes a new String long total = 0; for (String line : lines) total += line.split(" ").length; return total; } @Benchmark public long wordsByScan() { // walks the characters and counts where words start long total = 0; for (String line : lines) { boolean inWord = false; for (int i = 0; i < line.length(); i++) { boolean letter = line.charAt(i) != ' '; if (letter && !inWord) total++; inWord = letter; } } return total; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { var options = new OptionsBuilder() .include(WordCountBench.class.getName()) .addProfiler(GCProfiler.class) // the same as -prof gc on the command line .verbosity(VerboseMode.SILENT) .build(); System.out.printf("%-14s %12s %10s %14s %8s%n", "Benchmark", "ns/op", "error", "B/op", "error"); for (RunResult r : new Runner(options).run()) { var time = r.getPrimaryResult(); var bytes = r.getSecondaryResults().get("gc.alloc.rate.norm"); System.out.printf("%-14s %12.1f %10.1f %14.3f %8.3f%n", r.getParams().getBenchmark().replaceAll(".*\\.", ""), time.getScore(), time.getScoreError(), bytes.getScore(), bytes.getScoreError()); } } }

alt.title: WordCountBench.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l03 // WordCountBench.java measures with JMH, which needs Java classes in this lab. This Kotlin twin runs // the same two word counts written in Kotlin and reads the JVM's per-thread allocation counter // around 100,000 calls: the same bytes-per-call idea as JMH's gc.alloc.rate.norm. // Allocation is steady enough to count this way. Time is not (remember NanoLoop). import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory private val lines = Array(100) { "the report counts every word on line number $it" } fun wordsBySplit(): Long { var total = 0L for (line in lines) total += line.split(' ').size // Kotlin's split returns a List of new Strings return total } fun wordsByScan(): Long { var total = 0L for (line in lines) { var inWord = false for (c in line) { val letter = c != ' ' if (letter && !inWord) total++ inWord = letter } } return total } private val threads = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() as com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean private var sink = 0L // results go somewhere the JIT can't ignore private inline fun bytesPerCall(calls: Int, block: () -> Long): Double { repeat(50_000) { sink += block() } // warm up first, so C2 code is measured val before = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes repeat(calls) { sink += block() } return (threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes - before).toDouble() / calls } fun main() { val split = bytesPerCall(100_000) { wordsBySplit() } val scan = bytesPerCall(100_000) { wordsByScan() } println("wordsBySplit: %10.3f B/op".format(split)) println("wordsByScan: %10.3f B/op".format(scan)) println("(checksum $sink)") }

try.expect: wordsBySplit allocates about 54,400 bytes per call with a small error, while its time error is huge on a busy machine. wordsByScan allocates almost nothing (under 1 byte, which is JMH's own rounding). The Kotlin twin prints exactly 56000.000 and 0.000 B/op. Kotlin's split is a different function from Java's: it returns a List of new strings, not an array, so its count is a little higher. The scan allocates nothing in either language.

compare.title: Constants that get baked into the bytecode

java.title: Java
java.html: class Inputs { private final long words = 1_234; // constant initializer: javac copies the value private final long fromCtor; // assigned in the constructor: a real field read long plain = 1_234; // what a benchmark input should be static final long WORDS_PER_MINUTE = 238; // copied by javac, and known to the JIT Inputs(long v) { fromCtor = v; } }

kotlin.title: Kotlin
kotlin.html: const val WORDS_PER_MINUTE = 238L // copied by kotlinc; WORDS_PER_MINUTE * 2 becomes 476 open class Inputs(val fromCtor: Long) { // a real field read val words = 1_234L // NOT copied: kotlinc reads the field var plain = 1_234L // what a benchmark input should be }

compare.note: Java copies any final field with a constant initializer into the code that uses it, instance fields included. Kotlin copies only const val. A Kotlin val words = 1_234L compiles to a getfield, as javap shows, so kotlinc doesn't fold it. Use var in a Kotlin benchmark anyway, because it tells the next reader "this is an input". Both compilers also do arithmetic on constants themselves: in Kotlin, WORDS_PER_MINUTE * 2 compiled to ldc2_w 476. In either language, a benchmark that reads only constants measures the JIT's arithmetic, not yours.

worked.title: Turn a nanoTime test into a benchmark you can trust

steps.say: A pull request (a proposed change, waiting for review) claims the new word counter is "3x faster", based on this test. Spot the problems before reading on.
steps.code: @Test void newCounterIsFaster() { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) NewCounter.count("the quick report"); // constant input, result dropped long newNs = System.nanoTime() - t0; t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) OldCounter.count("the quick report"); long oldNs = System.nanoTime() - t0; assertTrue(newNs * 3 < oldNs); }

alt.html: @Test fun `new counter is faster`() { var t0 = System.nanoTime() repeat(1_000_000) { NewCounter.count("the quick report") } // constant input, result dropped val newNs = System.nanoTime() - t0 t0 = System.nanoTime() repeat(1_000_000) { OldCounter.count("the quick report") } val oldNs = System.nanoTime() - t0 assertTrue(newNs * 3 < oldNs) }

steps.say: Four problems. The results are dropped (dead code). The input is a constant (folding). The first loop warms up the JVM, so the second inherits a warm JVM and a mixed profile. And a timing assertion in a unit test fails at random on a busy build machine. Move the comparison to JMH, with the input in a non-final field.
steps.code: @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Fork(3) public class CounterBench { String line = "the quick report"; // 1. a non-final input @Benchmark public long oldCounter() { return OldCounter.count(line); } // 2. returned @Benchmark public long newCounter() { return NewCounter.count(line); } @Benchmark public void baseline() { } // 3. the floor to compare with }

alt.html: @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Fork(3) open class CounterBench { var line = "the quick report" // 1. a non-final input @Benchmark fun oldCounter(): Long = OldCounter.count(line) // 2. returned @Benchmark fun newCounter(): Long = NewCounter.count(line) @Benchmark fun baseline() {} // 3. the floor to compare with }

steps.say: Add a @Param so the input isn't one magic line, and turn on -prof gc so you get a steady second number. Self-check: why does @Param take strings? (Answer: JMH sets the field from text, one run per value, so the values also show up in the results table.)
steps.code: @Param({"a", "the quick report", "a much longer line with many more words in it"}) String line;

alt.html: @Param("a", "the quick report", "a much longer line with many more words in it") var line = ""

steps.say: Read the result with the error column, and check the baseline first. If newCounter sits on the baseline, it measures nothing. If the error bars of the two counters overlap, "3x faster" isn't proven. And if newCounter allocates 0 B/op where oldCounter allocates 160, that's a result you can put in the pull request whatever the timer says.
steps.code:
Benchmark                              (line)  Mode  Cnt   Score   Error   Units
CounterBench.newCounter                    ...  avgt   15   ...     ...   ns/op
CounterBench.newCounter:gc.alloc.rate.norm ...  avgt   15   ...     ...    B/op

lab.title: Fix three broken benchmarks
steps: The three benchmarks measure the report service's ReadingMath.readingSeconds(words), the reading time from lesson 1. Run the tests. Five of six fail; the sixth only checks that the classes are still JMH benchmarks. The tests never time anything: they call your benchmark methods and inspect them with reflection.
DeadResultBench: make seconds() hand its result to JMH.
ConstantInputBench: make words an input the compiler can't know. Keep the field name, because the test sets it to other values and expects seconds() to follow.

ColdBatchBench: move building the batch into a @Setup method that runs once per fork, and keep only the adding up in totalSeconds(). Then give it real warm-up (at least 3 iterations) and at least one fork.
Run the tests until all six pass. Optional: copy one fixed class into src/demo/.../l03, give it a main like TrapsBench's, and run it before and after your fix.
hints: For DeadResultBench, changing void to long and adding return is the whole fix. A Blackhole parameter also passes, but one result reads better as a return value.
For ConstantInputBench, look at javap -c -p on the compiled class before and after. Before: ldc2_w 1234. After: getfield words.

In ColdBatchBench, add a long[] batch field and a @Setup(Level.Trial) public void buildBatch() method. Don't use Level.Invocation: it runs setup around every single call and distorts short benchmarks.
@Fork(0) runs the benchmark inside the JVM that launched it, with that JVM's profile and garbage. Use at least 1, ideally 2 or more.

drill.title: Write a correct benchmark from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a JMH benchmark that measures ReadingMath.readingSeconds(words) over a 1,000-document batch built by Fixtures.batch(1000). Include the state, setup, warm-up, measurement, forks and mode. Then check it against the answer: is the batch built outside the measurement, is the result consumed, and are the inputs non-final fields?

answer.html: @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.MICROSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 5, time = 1) @Measurement(iterations = 5, time = 1) @Fork(2) public class BatchReadingBench { int size = 1_000; long[] batch; // non-final input @Setup(Level.Trial) // once per fork, not measured public void build() { batch = Fixtures.batch(size); } @Benchmark public long totalSeconds() { long total = 0; for (long words : batch) total += ReadingMath.readingSeconds(words); return total; // consumed by JMH } }

alt.html: @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.MICROSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 5, time = 1) @Measurement(iterations = 5, time = 1) @Fork(2) open class BatchReadingBench { var size = 1_000 lateinit var batch: LongArray // non-final input @Setup(Level.Trial) // once per fork, not measured fun build() { batch = Fixtures.batch(size) } @Benchmark fun totalSeconds(): Long { var total = 0L for (words in batch) total += ReadingMath.readingSeconds(words) return total // consumed by JMH } }

recap: A hand-made nanoTime loop measures the optimizer: dead code is removed (0.0000 ns/op), constants are folded, the first rounds run cold, and loops get unrolled. Whether a call disappears can even change between JDKs.
JMH generates the measuring loop, runs warm-up iterations it throws away, then measurement iterations in fresh JVMs (@Fork), and reports a score with an error.
Return every result or consume it in a Blackhole, and read inputs from non-final @State fields. Java copies a final field with a constant initializer straight into your method.
Compare against an empty baseline() benchmark: anything that scores like it is measuring nothing.
-prof gc gives gc.alloc.rate.norm, bytes per operation. It stays steady on a busy machine, so it's the number to check in CI; time isn't.
The limit: a benchmark measures a small piece of code on its own, usually on one thread. It can't tell you which piece of a real program is slow; that's the profilers' job in lessons 5 and 6.

explain.prompt: A teammate pastes "new word counter: 12 ns/op, old one: 40 ns/op" from a loop timed with System.nanoTime(). Explain, in your own words, why you don't trust it yet and what you'd ask for instead.
explain.answer: A hand-made loop measures whatever the JIT left behind. If the counter's result isn't used, C2 can delete the work. If the input is a constant, it can fold it. And the first loop runs partly in the interpreter, while the second runs in a warmed-up JVM with a profile the first one shaped. So 12 against 40 might measure dead code, warm-up order or OSR. I'd ask for a JMH benchmark with the input text in a non-final @State field, the count returned, an empty baseline to compare with, a few forks so each run gets a fresh JVM, and -prof gc so we also get bytes per operation. That number is steady enough to trust and to check in CI.

deeper.html:
Three more JMH features are worth knowing before you need them.

@State(Scope.Benchmark) shares one state object across all benchmark threads, and @Threads(4) or @Group runs several threads at once. That's how you measure contention, threads getting in each other's way: for example 4 threads incrementing one AtomicLong against one LongAdder. Lesson 4 talks about why those differ.

Mode.SampleTime records the times of individual calls and prints percentiles (p50, p99, p99.9), which fits questions about slow requests better than an average does. Mode.SingleShotTime measures one call per iteration, which suits questions about cold starts.

JMH pads @State objects automatically against one kind of interference between threads: the JMH false-sharing sample says "@States are automatically padded", but "This padding does not extend to the State internals". Fields inside your state object can still share a cache line, which is lesson 4's topic.

If you want to see what C2 really did to a benchmark, -prof perfasm prints the busiest generated machine code next to the hardware counters. It needs Linux perf and the hsdis disassembler. Without it, the cheap check is the one you already know: put an empty baseline next to every benchmark, and be suspicious of anything that scores like it.
